title: I built a free tool that reads trading chart screenshots and finds support & resistance in seconds. Looking for honest feedback
author: charttrader_lb

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: levels from real candles beat reading pixels off a screenshot by a mile. how do you rank them, by number of touches or by how much volume traded at the level?

replies.author: charttrader_lb
replies.body:
Thanks, that's exactly why I went with real candles 🙂

Honest answer: right now it's swing-based, not volume-based. It finds swing highs and lows (pivots with 3 candles on each side), then clusters pivots that sit within about half an ATR of each other into one level. The level price is the average of that cluster, and the number of pivots in it is the touch count.

For display it currently shows the nearest 2–3 levels above and below price, so it's ranked by distance, not by touches. Touches are tracked but don't change the order yet.

Volume only comes in as a confirmation factor (is the latest candle's volume above its 20-candle average?), not as volume-at-price.

Your question made me think, though: weighting levels by touches plus volume traded around them (a simple volume profile) would probably rank the strong ones much better than distance alone. Which do you trust more in your own trading, touches or volume?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: touches, but only real ones. a wick that tags the level by a cent shouldn't count like a bounce of half an ATR, and volume at price breaks ties. it's testable too: does a 3-touch level hold on the next retest more often than a 1-touch one? I wanted that answer for my own levels, so I built Quantradin (quantradin.com). it's free and runs on paper.

replies.author: charttrader_lb
replies.body:
That's a really good rule. A wick tagging the level by a cent and a clean half-ATR bounce shouldn't carry the same weight, agreed.

So I'm going to change how touches count: only a pivot whose reaction moves at least ~0.5 ATR away from the level counts as a real touch, levels get ranked by those weighted touches first, and volume traded around the level breaks ties. Distance from price becomes the last tiebreaker, not the main one.

And yes, the hold-rate test is the right way to prove it. I'll run "3-touch vs 1-touch: does it hold on the next retest?" on daily data across crypto, forex and indices and share the numbers here.

Quantradin looks interesting, congrats on shipping it. Mine is aimed at a slightly different moment: you're staring at a chart (any screenshot, any broker, or a live symbol) and want the key levels, scenarios and the invalidation point in a few seconds before deciding anything.

If anyone here wants to try it on a chart they're watching this week, I'd love to hear where the levels look wrong: https://aichartanalyser.com/?utm_source=reddit

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that'll clean it up a lot. I'd put a time limit on the reaction too, otherwise a level that took 40 bars to drift half an ATR away scores the same as one that snapped back in three.

replies.author: charttrader_lb
replies.body: Good call, the reaction has to happen within a few bars to count, not drift there over 40. Adding that. Thanks for the sharp feedback, really helpful.

comments.author: Kamla_AI
comments.body:
I’m part of the Kamla team.



How does it handle an older screenshot when the user also enters a live symbol? I’d want to know whether the levels refer to the screenshot’s date or the current market. Showing the timeframe and data timestamp beside the result would make that easier to interpret, especially if someone uploads a chart saved earlier in the week.

comments.author: investigatormaker
comments.body:
Support and resistance is where traders disagree most, so much of the honest feedback will be people saying they would draw the lines elsewhere. Showing why each level was picked (touches, swing highs and lows, timeframe) lets them judge the method rather than argue with the output. Worth testing before they do: a cropped price axis or a log-scale chart, since reading prices off a screenshot depends on those labels.
